For a 3-D printed rocket combustion-chamber liner, GRCop-42 or GRCop-84?

Abstract
A summary of 20 published papers, with 233 values plotted from them (60 from tables, 7 from the text, 166 from digitized figures, plus 28 points of a published fit). 6 relevant papers could not be obtained.
Methods, in order: 1. microstructure: read from text → 2. tensile strength against temperature (wrought curves, printed room-temperature tests) → 3. thermal conductivity against temperature (wrought curves, printed laser-flash data, a published fit) → 4. room-temperature yield and tensile strength for every printed and wrought condition → 5. hot fire: read from text
TL;DR

GRCop-42, which is where NASA moved for printed chambers: GRCop-84 is stronger below about 600 °C, the two are close above it (wrought data), and GRCop-42 conducts 5-15 % more heat and prints about 20 % faster [5]. Both are copper hardened by the same Cr2Nb particles; GRCop-42 (Cu-4Cr-2Nb, at%) has about half as much of them as GRCop-84 (Cu-8Cr-4Nb) [12]. In a printed part, porosity, surface finish and heat treatment move the properties as much as the alloy does [16] [15] [19]. Both alloys have been fired as printed liners, but never side by side.

Then, closed until you open it: Details: every plotted value and its source

Introduction

Why the question matters and what was read to answer it.

GRCop-42 and GRCop-84 are NASA copper alloys developed for the liners of regeneratively cooled rocket combustion chambers, which need high strength and high conductivity at elevated temperature [12]. For a liner, thermal conductivity and low-cycle fatigue (LCF) dominate the choice, because the constrained hot wall is strained by 1 % or more on every firing [5]. A copper liner fired with hydrogen and oxygen can also suffer blanching, surface damage from repeated oxidation and reduction of the hot wall [5]. Both alloys are now 3-D printed, by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF, a laser melting thin layers of powder) or laser-powder directed energy deposition (DED, powder blown into a moving laser spot), and the parts are usually hot isostatically pressed (HIP, held hot under high gas pressure) to close porosity [19]. Electrical conductivity is quoted as a percent of the International Annealed Copper Standard (% IACS, where pure annealed copper is 100 %).

Both alloys are two phases: a copper matrix and particles of Cr2Nb, a Laves-phase intermetallic compound that forms in the melt as the cubic C15 structure [11]. The particles strengthen the copper; GRCop-42 was made by halving them, "to trade mechanical properties for improved thermal conductivity" [12]. The open question is how much of the published difference between the two alloys survives in printed parts at service temperature.

20 papers were read for this summary, found through 10 searches (OpenAlex). 6 more papers judged relevant could not be obtained; they are listed at the end with their DOIs. Every figure below is drawn only from values recorded with where they appear in the paper (table, page or figure); the full list is under Details.

Results from the papers

Each question below is answered from the papers' own numbers.

(a) What is different inside the two alloys?

Twice the Cr2Nb in GRCop-84; printing makes the particles small

Where the numbers come from
Method
Read from the papers' text; no plotted values for this question.
Inputs
Chen 2023, Zhong 2023, Yang 2022, Pan 2024
Tells us
GRCop-84 carries about twice the Cr2Nb of GRCop-42; printing makes the particles far smaller than casting.
Assumes
cast and sintered Cu-Cr-Nb papers describe the same Cr2Nb phase as printed GRCop
  • Extracting and weighing the particles from printed material gives 12.70 wt% for GRCop-84 against 6.64 wt% for GRCop-42, close to the nominal 12.3 and 6.1 wt% Cr2Nb (Table 4) [12]. In printed GRCop-42 most particles are under 1 µm across [12].
  • Cast and slowly cooled (1 °C/s), the same compositions grow particles of about 200 µm in Cu-8Cr-4Nb and 60 µm in Cu-4Cr-2Nb, because Cr2Nb starts to form at about 1590 °C in the richer alloy against 1450 °C in the leaner one [14]. The papers read do not test why printed particles are sub-micron; the far faster cooling of a laser melt pool is the likely cause.
  • Cr2Nb from the melt is the cubic C15 structure; a second, hexagonal C14 form precipitates only on aging near 600 °C, as nanometer particles [11].
  • Particle size controls strength. In a sintered Nb-lean Cu-Cr-Nb alloy, aging at 600 °C for 1 h raised tensile strength from 384 to 439 MPa, while 1000 °C for 1 h coarsened the particles to 1.13 µm and dropped it to 277 MPa [17]. That alloy is not GRCop, so the numbers show the direction, not GRCop's values.

(b) Which alloy is stronger, and does the gap last at service temperature?

GRCop-84 is stronger cold, the gap closes at service temperature

Where the numbers come from
Method
Values typed from the papers' tables and text, each checked against the printed page; curves were read from the paper's vector drawing: the axis ticks were located in the drawing itself, their values read off the figure, each label checked to sit on its tick, and the drawn curve converted to numbers at fixed temperature steps.
Inputs
Gradl 2019 [5]: Fig. 6, digitized; Table 3; Fig. 7, digitized; Mahtabi 2025 [20]: text, p. 9979; Seltzman & Wukitch 2021 [9]: Table 6; Demeneghi 2024 [15]: Table 3; Demeneghi 2022 [10]: Table 7; Demeneghi 2025 [19]: text (Discussion)
Tells us
GRCop-84 is stronger cold; the wrought curves meet near 600 °C, and printed room-temperature values spread by more than the gap between the alloys.
Assumes
wrought curves stand in for printed material above room temperature; a digitized point is the authors' drawn curve, not a single test
  • Wrought: "At lower temperatures, mainly below 600 °C (1112 °F), GRCop-84 is clearly stronger than GRCop-42", and the two have "essentially the same strength" above 600 °C [5].
  • HIPed L-PBF at room temperature on the same Concept Laser M2: GRCop-84 390 MPa UTS / 208 MPa yield / 30 % elongation; GRCop-42 359 / 173 MPa / 32.2 % (Table 2) [4].
  • L-PBF from multiple vendors, room temperature: GRCop-84 444 ± 2 MPa UTS and 256 ± 7 MPa yield, GRCop-42 348 ± 11 MPa and 200 ± 6 MPa [20]. That paper does not state the specimens' heat treatment in the sections read, so these numbers should not be set beside the HIPed values as if the condition matched.
  • Thin GRCop-42 walls lose about 40 % of their yield strength in HIP: 266-281 MPa as built, 161-163 MPa after [15]. HIPed DED GRCop-42 walls are weaker still, 96-121 MPa yield [10].
  • Creep: a refit of old wrought NASA data gives Cu-4Cr-2Nb 3.5-3.8 times the creep strain of Cu-8Cr-4Nb after 2 h at 927 K (654 °C), in both creep models fitted, at 60.8 MPa [2]. Wrought LCF at room temperature, 400 and 600 °C: GRCop-42 ran a lower stress range than GRCop-84 at the same strain, with similar plastic strain per cycle [5]. No LCF or creep comparison of printed material was found.

(c) How much more heat does GRCop-42 conduct?

GRCop-42 wins, by an amount the sources disagree on

Where the numbers come from
Method
Values typed from the papers' tables and text, each checked against the printed page; curves digitized as described in (a).
Inputs
Gradl 2019 [5]: Fig. 1, digitized; Fig. 15, digitized; Chen 2023 [12]: text (Section 3.1 fit)
Tells us
GRCop-42 conducts 13 to 20 % more than standard wrought GRCop-84 and 5 to 8 % more in the early printed samples; iron content and the build move the numbers by as much.
Assumes
a digitized point is the authors' drawn curve, not a single test
  • Wrought, room temperature: 85 % IACS for GRCop-42 against 75 % IACS for GRCop-84 [5].
  • L-PBF, laser flash: "a 5-8% increase in conductivity" for GRCop-42 over GRCop-84 on early development samples [5].
  • Two later papers state the advantage as "about 15 %" [12] and "about 10 %" [19]. Both relay earlier references in their introductions; neither measures it.
  • L-PBF GRCop-42 from eight vendors fits k(T) = -39.86 T^3 + 4.17 T^2 + 0.97 T + 329.14 W/(m K), T in K/1000, over 25-700 °C, with about ±4 % scatter against ±3 % instrument uncertainty [12].
  • Where a GRCop-84 liner is printed onto a nickel-alloy jacket, nickel mixed into the copper drops the local conductivity to 68-118 W/(m K), a third of the alloy's own [13].

(d) Do process and heat treatment matter as much as the alloy?

GRCop-42 prints faster; both are limited by pores, surfaces and joints

Where the numbers come from
Method
Values typed from the papers' tables and text, each checked against the printed page.
Inputs
Gradl 2019 [5]: Table 3; Mahtabi 2025 [20]: text, p. 9979; Seltzman & Wukitch 2021 [9]: Table 6; Table 7; Gradl 2019 [4]: Table 2; Demeneghi 2024 [16]: Table 3; Demeneghi 2024 [15]: Table 3; Demeneghi 2022 [10]: Table 7
Tells us
Heat treatment moves printed GRCop-84 from about 210 to 785 MPa yield; at a matched condition the two alloys differ by 25 to 60 MPa.
Assumes
the papers' own numbers are right
  • GRCop-42 parameters cut L-PBF build time by about 20 % relative to GRCop-84, whose 30 µm layers could take 28 days for a 10.8 in part; GRCop-42 powder was easier for vendors to make to specification [5].
  • L-PBF and DED give different GRCop-42 properties: thin walls showed 145-165 MPa yield by L-PBF against 101-102 MPa by DED [16]. HIP leaves DED walls essentially pore-free, but the wavy as-deposited layers cut the elongation of vertical specimens to 19-30 %, against 37-48 % for horizontal ones [10].
  • Porosity sets fatigue life: as-built L-PBF GRCop-42 walls failed near 10^5 cycles, HIPed walls ran out at 10^6 [15].
  • Heat treatment dominates GRCop-84 strength: 492 MPa yield as printed, 291 MPa after 900 °C for 5 h, and 785 ± 36 MPa after 450 °C for 3 h (Tables 6 and 7) [9]. Brazing, a 935 °C excursion, did not significantly change wrought GRCop-84's properties [1]; printed GRCop-84 loses strength at 900 °C, from 492 to 291 MPa yield [9].
  • Printed GRCop-84 is Ra 3.3 µm on vertical walls and 11.6 µm on top surfaces; vibratory finishing reaches 0.45 µm [7]. On one machine it held 10-40 µm accuracy and printed 150 µm fins, but walls thinner than 1 mm warped [8]. These come from fusion-reactor waveguides, so they bound a liner's channels rather than describe one.
  • Joining the liner to a nickel-alloy jacket is a weak point for either alloy. IN718 printed onto GRCop-42 left lack-of-fusion at the interface, and GRCop-42 printed onto IN718 mixed and formed alpha-Cr [18]. LENS-printed GRCop-84 was the weak side of an IN718 joint, 110 MPa in shear [6].

(e) Has either alloy been proven in a fired chamber?

Both alloys have run as printed liners, in different tests

Where the numbers come from
Method
Read from the papers' text; no plotted values for this question.
Inputs
Gradl 2019, Gradl 2017, Gradl 2019, Demeneghi 2025
Tells us
Both have run in hot fire as printed liners; no test fires the two under the same conditions.
Assumes
hot-fire counts are as each NASA paper reports them
  • GRCop-42: 188 tests and 8,030 s on L-PBF chambers, with no blanching [5].
  • GRCop-84: NASA's first L-PBF chambers ran 23 starts and 2,365 s of LOX/hydrogen [3]; bimetallic GRCop-84 chambers with a deposited jacket ran 11 starts and 475 s [4].
  • One L-PBF GRCop-42 chamber split on its 10th start at build-interruption lines, where post-HIP porosity reached 1.9 % and oxygen exceeded specification; interrupted test bars were sound, so the authors fault process control, not the alloy [19].

Caveats and next steps

What this search did not settle.

No paper read here fires printed GRCop-42 and GRCop-84 under the same conditions, or compares them in creep or LCF at service temperature (500-800 °C); the statements that the alloys match above 600 °C and differ in LCF stress range rest on wrought material [5]. Six relevant papers could not be obtained and are listed at the end with their DOIs: a 2021 NASA hot-fire paper on printed liners of both alloys, a 2023 study of precipitate size in both alloys as powder and as printed, an independent 2020 review of Cu-Cr-Nb alloys, and three process papers (GRCop-42 by green laser and by DED, and a 2018 characterization of printed GRCop-84). The first two bear directly on the gaps above.
